title: When AI Takes Away the Easy Work, Does Work Get Harder?
summary: How does AI change emotional labor at work? Explore how automation can concentrate demanding tasks and what organizations can do to support employees.
body_markdown:
It’s mid-afternoon in a busy contact center. A customer service advisor has just finished a difficult call, and the next one is already waiting. This customer has tried the app, searched the FAQs, and gone back and forth with the chatbot to no avail. Their problem is unusual and falls outside the scenarios those tools were designed to handle. So, by the time they reach the advisor, they’re frustrated and need an answer nobody has scripted.
The next call is no easier.


This is the work advisors on the phone are left with when self-service handles the simple contacts: one hard call after another.


In many respects, this is exactly what automation is meant to achieve. Straightforward inquiries get resolved without a person, customers get quicker answers, and advisors spend less time on repeat requests. But the job has changed, too. The password resets, account updates, and routine questions that used to break up a shift are disappearing, and with them the breathing room between difficult conversations.


There’s a familiar promise around AI at work: automate repetitive tasks and give people more time to focus on higher-value activities. On paper, it makes perfect sense. Yet time saved and effort saved are not always the same thing. When AI removes routine tasks, it can concentrate emotional labor and other demanding work into a larger share of the working day. We may automate the easy parts of a job without making the job itself any easier.


## The Hidden Value of Easy Work


Not all work asks the same of us. Some tasks involve difficult conversations, complex decisions, or problems without an obvious answer. Others are more routine: completing administrative tasks, sending a standard email, updating a record, or processing a straightforward request.


We tend to see routine tasks as low-value work and, understandably, they’re often the first things we look to automate. But they may serve another purpose, too. Moving between harder and easier activities changes the pace of the day, and after a difficult interaction or a period of intense concentration, a simpler task can give us a chance to reset.


**I think of these tasks as mental palate cleansers.** We rarely attach much value to them because that value doesn’t appear on a productivity dashboard. Yet removing them can change the experience of a working day considerably.


Imagine four hours of an eight-hour day are spent on genuinely demanding work, with easier activities scattered between them. Now imagine AI removes many of those routine activities. Perhaps that creates time for learning, research, or thinking. Or perhaps we simply fill the space with more of the work AI could not do.


Over time, four hours of demanding work becomes five, six, or seven. The process may be more efficient, and the employees more productive, but the job itself has become more intense.


It can increase emotional labor, too: the effort employees use to manage difficult interactions while responding professionally and effectively. When automation resolves the easy customer inquiries, advisors may spend more time speaking to people who are frustrated, worried, or angry. In other settings, people may spend more of their day making difficult judgments where the answer is uncertain, and the consequences matter.


None of this means we should preserve tedious work because people need a break. There are better ways to create recovery than asking someone to update a spreadsheet. The point is that if routine work once created natural changes of pace, removing it without thinking about what takes its place can create unintended consequences.


## How AI Efficiency Changes Emotional Labor at Work


Customer service makes this particularly easy to see. As self-service and automation get better at resolving straightforward inquiries, fewer of those inquiries need to reach an advisor. That can be good for customers and organizations alike.


But the customers who still need a person are more likely to be those whose problem couldn’t be solved through the automated route. Their circumstances may be unusual, their problem complicated, or their situation emotionally charged. As a result, automation can reduce contact volumes while increasing the emotional labor required in the interactions that remain.


**We have reduced work in one sense but potentially increased its intensity in another.**


Radiology offers another telling example. AI promised to reduce the burden on radiologists by supporting parts of the medical-imaging workflow and improving productivity. Yet the emerging evidence suggests a more complicated picture, with researchers reporting increases in burnout rather than the clear net improvements that might have been expected from greater automation.


New technology changes how people work and can require them to decide[when to trust an algorithm and when to question it](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/blog/trust-ai-capability-vs-scale/) . Greater efficiency may also allow more cases to be processed. Saving time on an individual task doesn’t necessarily mean the person doing the job ends up with more breathing room.


This doesn’t mean AI causes burnout. It means that measuring time saved on individual tasks only tells part of the story. We also need to understand what the job looks like once those tasks disappear.


## Designing the Work AI Leaves Behind


If AI changes the mix of tasks within a role, organizations need to design around the new job rather than assume it is simply the old job with some activities removed.


That means thinking about both capability and capacity. If employees increasingly deal with situations AI cannot resolve, those situations are likely to require greater judgment, problem-solving, interpersonal skill, and emotional labor.


Training, therefore, needs to go beyond showing employees how to use a new AI tool. Organizations need to identify the behaviors and capabilities needed for the work AI leaves behind and offer the right guidance, coaching, and support.


There is another, potentially more uncomfortable question, too: **does every minute AI saves need to become another minute of productive output?**


That capacity could go somewhere else rather than into the same work. Organizations might reinvest it in learning, coaching, collaboration, or recovery after particularly demanding work. Or they might use it to resolve complex cases more thoroughly, reduce repeat contacts, identify recurring problems, improve processes, or strengthen quality.


Each of these can support productivity by making good performance sustainable. The risk comes when efficiency gains are treated simply as an opportunity to increase utilization, particularly when the work that remains is more cognitively or emotionally demanding.


## Redesigning the Human Side of AI


For organizations implementing AI, this is more than a theoretical question. **I have seen it firsthand** . In some operations, advisors who were used to handling only a few emotionally difficult interactions each day found themselves dealing with a much greater concentration of distressed customers. In others, advisors faced challenging retention conversations with customers experiencing significant price increases.


This is where behavioral science has a significant role to play. We can understand what the redesigned job now asks of people, identify the behaviors and capabilities it requires, and develop the skills, language, and practical tools that help people respond effectively and confidently.


I have also seen what can happen when we get that right. In projects I’ve led, we’ve seen reductions in absenteeism and burnout alongside increases in participants’ self-confidence and self-efficacy. That matters because AI transformation is usually judged on how well the technology and processes are redesigned.[The human side of the job needs the same attention](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/blog/customer-experience-ai-and-human-connection/) .


That means looking beyond productivity alone to whether people have the capability, confidence, and support to perform the new role sustainably.


Much of the conversation about AI asks how much time the technology can save. We should be equally interested in how organizations use that reclaimed time. If automation removes some of the easiest tasks but leaves people with a greater concentration of the hardest ones, filling every newly available minute may improve efficiency while[making the job less sustainable.](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/blog/wellbeing-at-scale-the-impact-of-employee-wellbeing-initiatives/)


**AI can take work away from people, but that doesn’t automatically mean it reduces the load they carry.**
